rules.reason: Request or response bodies of the paths or webhooks scope are object schemas that generation types inline although their schema definitions get models ({inline_object_bodies}), such as a type array [object, null]. With them modeled as definitions, each body gets that model, and a document whose only bodies are such schemas generates models instead of failing with 'Models not found in the input data'. The same principle gives a component written as a $ref to a recursive schema with sibling keywords the root model a definitions entry of that schema gets, as the 20261027 presets do.
evidence: OpenAPI request body {type: [object, null], additionalProperties: {...}} under --openapi-scopes paths: 'Models not found in the input data' without the option, a PetsPostRequest root model of dict[str, ...] | None with it
OpenAPI response body of the same shape: 'Models not found in the input data' without the option, a PetsGetResponse root model with it
nullable_map_value_types.yaml test input: the POST /scores request body [object, null] gains ScoresPostRequest; every other model is unchanged

rules.reason: Schemas set constraints that the generated type enforces itself ({redundant_constraints}): a const or an enum beside a length or number keyword its values meet, or exactly one number bound equal to 0, which --use-non-positive-negative-number-constrained-types turns into a class such as NonNegativeInt. With redundant constraints omitted, the field does not write them again beside the type, and a const branch whose constraints its value meets stays a Literal instead of a root model.
evidence: {type: string, const: abc, minLength: 1} under --use-annotated: Literal['abc'] instead of Annotated[Literal['abc'], Field(min_length=1)]
{type: [integer, null], minimum: 0} under --use-annotated and --use-non-positive-negative-number-constrained-types: NonNegativeInt | None instead of Annotated[NonNegativeInt | None, Field(ge=0)]

rules.reason: Pydantic validates in lax mode, which coerces input into the {coercible_scalars} integer, number and boolean schemas: it accepts the string "5" and true as integers, "1.5" as a number, and "true" or 1 as booleans. Strict types reject such input. Whether to accept it depends on the project's clients, not on the schema; strict int also rejects 5.0, which JSON Schema counts as an integer, so leave int out to accept it.
evidence: 11 JSON documents for integer, number, boolean and string properties, 6 of them invalid: lax mode accepted 5 invalid ones; with int float bool, 0 accepted and 1 valid one rejected (5.0 as an integer); with float bool, 2 accepted ("5" and true as integers) and none rejected
